lead: Both readings are about recognizing the one Lord. Paul pleads with the Corinthians not to split into parties around their preachers, because Christ is not divided and it was not Paul who was crucified for them. At Emmaus two disciples recognize the risen Jesus in the breaking of the bread and run back to the community in Jerusalem. The Lord is known at the table, and he gathers those who were scattered.

set: Paul founded the Church at Corinth, a busy port city of Greece, around AD 50–51, and wrote this letter a few years later from Ephesus (16:8). He has heard from “Chloe's people”, probably members of her household, that the community is breaking into groups, each attached to a favourite teacher. This is the first problem he takes up, and it shapes the whole letter.
str: vv. 11–12: the report and the slogans.
vv. 13–16: three questions, and Paul's thanks that he baptized so few.
v. 17: his mission: to preach the Cross.
kw: Literally “tears”, as in a torn garment. It is the root of our word schism. Paul is not speaking yet of separate Churches but of factions inside one community.
The verb means to mend or restore. Mark uses it of James and John mending their nets (Mark 1:19). Unity is something to be repaired with patience, like a net, so that it can hold.
The Aramaic name of Peter, meaning “rock”. Paul uses it often. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who taught at Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–28).
vv: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you be in agreement and that there be no divisions among you,
Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
Each question expects the answer no. The Church belongs to the one who died for her, not to the one who preached to her.
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the gospel, and not with eloquent wisdom, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied of its power.

Paul does not make light of Baptism; he has just said that they were baptized into Christ's name. He means that his own task was to preach, and that the power is in the Cross, not in the preacher's skill.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its decree on ecumenism by saying that Christ founded one Church, and that division openly contradicts his will, is a scandal to the world and harms the preaching of the Gospel (Unitatis Redintegratio 1). Paul's questions still speak to every parish and diocese: whenever we gather around a person rather than around Christ, the Body is torn.

r.h: Known in the breaking of the bread
set: On the day of the Resurrection two disciples, one named Cleopas, are walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sad and confused. A stranger joins them and explains the Scriptures about the Messiah (24:13–27). As evening falls they reach the village. This reading tells what happened at the table and afterwards.
str: vv. 28–29: he seems to go on; they urge him to stay.
vv. 30–31: at table he takes, blesses, breaks and gives; their eyes are opened; he vanishes.
vv. 33–35: they return to Jerusalem; the Lord has appeared to Simon; they tell their story.
kw: The same verb that John uses for abiding. The disciples' prayer, “Stay with us”, has become one of the Church's best-loved prayers at evening.
The phrase the first Christians used for the Eucharist (Acts 2:42). Luke's four verbs, took, blessed, broke and gave, are the verbs of the feeding of the crowd (9:16) and of the Last Supper (22:19).
vv: But they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, because it is almost evening and the day is now nearly over.” So he went in to stay with them.
He does not force his company on them. He waits to be invited.
When he was at the table with them, he took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to them.
Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
The story moves in the same order as the Holy Qurbana: first the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken, then the mission.
ch: The Catechism lists “the breaking of bread” among the names of the Eucharist, the name by which the first Christians called their gatherings, and it points to Emmaus (CCC 1329). It describes the Eucharistic celebration as following the same movement as the paschal meal of the risen Jesus with his disciples: he walked with them, explained the Scriptures, and broke the bread (CCC 1347).

qa: Does Paul make light of Baptism when he thanks God that he baptized few?

No. He is thankful only because no one can now claim to belong to Paul's party. In the same letter he teaches that “in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (12:13). Baptism unites us to Christ, not to the minister who baptizes.
study: Around whom or what do I sometimes gather, instead of around Christ? What helps me mend the net of unity in my parish?
The disciples recognized Jesus only at the table. How can I prepare my heart so that I recognize him at the Holy Qurbana?
